headlines.title: Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses
headlines.summary: Amazon's $250 Ring Drone Cam flies from room to room to investigate suspicious activity, and can capture footage at night.
headlines.article_text: Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone, robot to patrol homes, businesses Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Amazon's Ring unveiled a flying indoor security drone and a patrolling robot for businesses. The $250 Ring Drone Cam flies from room to room to investigate suspicious activity, and can capture footage at night. The $1,000 Ring Rover Cam repurposes Amazon's Astro robot for deployment in workplaces, such as warehouses and offices. In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Amazon's Ring unveiled a flying indoor security camera that lets users autonomously check on their home. Ring Amazon 's Ring is going deeper into surveillance with an indoor drone for home monitoring and an autonomous robot designed to patrol businesses. The company on Tuesday unveiled the $250 Ring Drone Cam, a security camera that can fly from room to room, including upstairs, as well as capture footage during the day or at night. When an alarm or sensor on windows, doors and home security devices is triggered, the textbook-sized drone travels a pre-set path to investigate suspicious activity. Users can also deploy the drone at any time, the company said. At a demo in New York on Monday, Ring CEO Jamie Siminoff said the drone could be used as a home monitoring tool and as a crime "deterrent" due to the device's built-in LED lights. "If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window," Siminoff said. "You're probably not going to go into that house." The drone, which can fly up to eight minutes at a time before autonomously returning to its charging dock, has two plastic-encased propellers that emit a loud buzz when it's airborne. Ring devices have provided Amazon another avenue to grow its presence in the smart home beyond its Echo smart speakers and Eero routers, expanding in a market that Grand View Research estimates will top $200 billion in sales this year. It's equally fertile ground for Amazon rivals Apple and Google . Ring, which Amazon acquired in 2018 and is known for its doorbells, has been beset with privacy concerns , primarily due to its partnerships with police. Earlier this year, Ring faced renewed scrutiny over a controversial Super Bowl ad touting an AI pet-finding tool called "Search Party." It then canceled an integration with police tech provider Flock Safety , which has also faced widespread backlash over its automated license plate readers. Ring repurposed Amazon's Astro consumer robot, first unveiled in 2021, to be a business security device. Ring Ring first previewed its drone, then called the Always Home Cam , in 2020. Siminoff said he chose to hold off on releasing the device until Amazon could perfect the design, sensors and data processing. The company on Tuesday also debuted the $1,000 Ring Rover Cam. The device repurposes Amazon's Astro home robot , which had a short life as a business device and has seen few upgrades since its 2021 debut, for companies to patrol offices, warehouses and other workspaces. Ring said it "leveraged the best of Astro" to build the Ring Rover Cam, which it describes as a "purpose-built security robot." Similar to the Astro, the device is a display mounted on a two-wheeled base with an extendable periscope camera. It also features a "built-in siren," two-way audio and a "light tower" that shines onto the ceiling to help users keep track of its whereabouts. Siminoff said in an interview that the drone and the robot allow users to monitor multiple areas of their home or business with just one device. "People like indoor cameras, but they don't necessarily want them everywhere around their home," Siminoff said. Ring said privacy is the "default" mode for both the drone and the robot, which flash an LED light when they're recording. Siminoff said the drone can't fly outside per Federal Aviation Administration regulations, which restrict operating drones unless they're within a line of sight of a pilot. "We have told our customers not to do that because it's illegal," Siminoff said. "We've also put guardrails in there to make it so it doesn't fly outside." The Ring Drone Cam ships in the U.S. on Jan. 27, pending approval from the Federal Communications Commission, while the Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping to users on Dec. 16, the company said. headlines.title: How GM is trying to talk used car shoppers into buying new vehicles
headlines.summary: Automakers say that substantial shares of the customers walking into a dealership looking for certified used cars end up buying new. Here's how it works.
headlines.article_text: How GM is trying to talk used car shoppers into buying new vehicles Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Rising vehicle prices have been pushing many car buyers into the used market. General Motors is a key example of an automaker that's trying to convince some of those consumers to get new vehicles instead, in part by revamping its certified used vehicle program. GM made changes to the program, called CarBravo, in an effort to compete with Carvana and CarMax. In this article GM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 7:05 07:05 How automakers are getting used car buyers to pay for new CNBC Digital Original Video Affordability challenges are pushing some buyers out of the new vehicle market. Many are choosing used cars instead. In turn, automakers are looking for ways to compete with many of the online retailers grabbing market share in the used car market and trying to bring some of those customers back into a new vehicle. New vehicle sales tend to be more profitable for automakers, but reselling trade-ins as used vehicles is highly profitable for dealers. Used car prices are relatively strong, but newer online retailers such as Carvana and CarMax have made the market more competitive for dealers and other incumbent used car sellers. "The internet and technology and apps on our phone have changed every aspect of retail, and probably one of the slowest areas of retail to have adopted to online and digital shopping has been the auto industry," said Ivan Feinseth, partner, chief investment officer and director of research at Tigress Financial Partners. In an aerial view, Chevrolet trucks and SUVs are displayed on the sales lot at Stewart Chevrolet on Jan. 6, 2026 in Colma, California. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images GM's revamp General Motors is a key example of automakers' attempts to address this shifting market. The automaker has revamped its certified used vehicle program, which now operates under the CarBravo name. It's essentially an online portal through which Chevrolet, Buick and GMC dealers can list their certified used vehicles and make them available to customers all over the U.S. About 1,615 of GM's 3,700 dealers are enrolled in the program, according to the company. The only GM brand not involved is Cadillac, which maintains its own program. "Certified" used or "preowned" vehicles are used cars that have undergone a thorough inspection and reconditioning. They typically come with guarantees and warranties from the manufacturer. Many automakers have certified used programs for their own cars. But GM, as part of its revamp, is using CarBravo to certify vehicles made by other automakers. A lot of those cars arrive at dealerships as trade-ins, and often dealers will sell them to wholesale auctions, said John Fitzpatrick, senior manager of the CarBravo program. "Wholesaling doesn't bring nearly the revenue that selling it to a new customer does," he said. GM has said it is planning to net about 250,000 sales in its CarBravo program in 2026. Fitzpatrick said he doesn't expect that even half of those will end up being new car sales. But through CarBravo, the customer gets access to GM's dealership network for service, something Fitzpatrick says is a key differentiator between its program and growing online sellers. CarBravo vehicles come with various warranties, depending on the age and mileage on the car. GM said the program is driving more traffic into local dealerships, where purchases are typically finalized. That creates an opportunity to convert a used car shopper into a new car buyer. So far, the automaker said about 38% of the shoppers initially looking for used cars end up buying new. A customer who wants to buy a full-size truck can look on the website and compare used Chevrolet Silverados alongside used Ford F-150s and Ram 1500s, for example. The buyer might settle on a used truck from any of those brands, but a conversation with a dealer can push them in a different direction. "The customer picks up the phone, but in the back of their mind, they maybe always have been a traditional, more new car customer," Fitzpatrick said. "You've shown the customer, you're going to pay $500 [per month] for this used F-150, but you may pay $510 or $515 for this new Chevy," he said. "And now all of a sudden the customer says, yeah, maybe I can do that because I'd rather have that new vehicle than the used truck." While the average transaction price of a new vehicle is about $50,000, the average 3-year-old used car costs about $30,000 as of September, according to Cox Automotive. However, industry analysts say customers base their purchasing decisions on the cost of the monthly payment more than on the sticker price of the car. New cars often come with longer-term loan options than used ones, Feinseth said, which can result in lower monthly payments. "On a 1- or 2-year-old car, you may be only stuck with a 3- or 4-year loan," he said. "On a new car, you can get a 5-year, 6-year loan." The share of new car loans lasting 84 months hit a new record in the third quarter, at more than 1 in 4 loans, according to Edmunds. Meanwhile, used car prices in some affordable segments have risen, according to Cox Automotive, and about three quarters of consumers express some interest in certified cars. But the key is building the relationship with the customer, he said. About 50% of the buyers GM has gained through the program appear to be new to the brand, meaning there is no record of them in any of the automaker's customer databases. About 70% had never visited the dealership they ended up purchasing from. "The goal is really to get that customer engaged with the store, give them the option of building a relationship with the dealer," he said. "The dealer can really help the customer figure out what works for their budget." It's a boon for dealers too: Customers buying warranty-backed used cars often return to the dealership for service visits — which often account for about half of a dealership's profits. GM can also sell subscriptions to connected vehicle services, such as its OnStar, which provides safety, security and navigation services. "That is a big part of General Motors' business going forward, is to sell the software and subscription services like OnStar and eventually to the cars that are enabled with Super Cruise," GM's advanced driver-assistance system, Feinseth said. A detail view shows the lease price for a new vehicle for sale on a Ford dealership lot in Hawthorne, California, on February 18, 2026. Michael Yanow | Nurphoto | Getty Images GM's competition GM isn't the only automaker trying to use its certified preowned vehicle program to lure buyers. Detroit rival Ford Motor also certifies vehicles made by other manufacturers through its Ford Blue Advantage program. It is on track to do 450,000 total sales in 2026, more than GM's 250,000 target. It didn't specify how many of those buyers end up purchasing new vehicles. Toyota told CNBC in an email that about 40% of its used car shoppers end up buying new instead. Honda didn't give specifics about its program. But Lance Woelfer, American Honda's vice president of automobile sales, said conversions happen "probably every day at dealerships throughout the country." "But it also is more about that first interaction with the consumer," Woelfer said. "And there are people in any market that prefer to buy a used vehicle, but appreciate the confidence that a [certified preowned designation] can give them." Woelfer said those customers come back to get their vehicles serviced at a rate about 18% higher than someone who buys a non-certified used car. headlines.title: Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78, looks to start trading Nov. 19, sources say
headlines.summary: Anthropic's IPO is expected to come roughly five months after Elon Musk took SpaceX public in a record offering.
headlines.article_text: Anthropic sets price range of $70 to $78 in upcoming IPO Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming IPO at a price range between $70 to $78 per share. Should the offering take place in mid-November as expected, it will come roughly five months after SpaceX's record IPO. Anthropic has filed to trade on the Nasdaq under ticker symbol "ANT." In this article ANT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:35 06:35 Anthropic sets price range of $70 to $78 in upcoming IPO Squawk Box Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming IPO at a price range between $70 to $78 per share, according to an updated filing on Tuesday, bringing the five-year-old artificial intelligence lab a step closer to a potentially historic Nasdaq debut. The company is planning to price on Nov. 18 and trade on Nov. 19, according to people familiar with the details who were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Anthropic is targeting retail allocation of about 20%, the people said, a much higher percentage than the typical IPO, which is 5% to 10% for retail investors. At the high end of the range, Anthropic would net up to $64.35 billion in proceeds through the IPO. The company could end up being worth up to $1.405 trillion on a fully diluted basis, up from the $965 billion valuation it announced as part of a funding round in May. Anthropic said it has entered into an agreement with Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Google , Micron , Microsoft , Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company to purchase $26 billion of the company's Class N common stock in a private placement at a price per share equal to the IPO price. The shares sold in the private placement will not be registered in the offering and will not be subject to lock-up agreements with the underwriters, the company said. As Anthropic executives get set to pitch the offering to investors, they have to contend with a tumultuous political environment , following last week's midterm elections that included a Democratic sweep in Congress and the passage of numerous statewide ballot measures that could slow the AI buildout. They're also facing a public market that's grown increasingly skeptical of the AI trade on concern that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for companies that need it for costly infrastructure purchases. CNBC reported last week that some Anthropic investors were bracing for a lower valuation than had previously been expected. While Anthropic had been looking toward a $2 trillion valuation until recently, shareholders told CNBC that even $1.5 trillion is now in doubt, with one investor calling that number a "stretch." Should Anthropic reach the Nasdaq this month as planned, under ticker symbol "ANT," the debut would come roughly five months after SpaceX went public in a record offering that raised $85.7 billion. Elon Musk's reusable rocket and AI company has a market cap of just under $2 trillion, around its valuation at the time of the IPO. Institutional demand for Anthropic is even stronger than it was for SpaceX at this point in the process, the people said. The company's book is already covered at the $70 to $78 per share range on an allocable basis, they said. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the AI lab in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, and the company primarily sells its products and services to other businesses. On Monday, Anthropic introduced two new AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, the first time the company has released so-called "frontier" models since Amodei called to slow down the pace of AI development in September . Anthropic said the models went through rigorous safety and alignment testing, and that the company developed new evaluations and post-launch monitoring tools ahead of the release. For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said. Anthropic said in its amended filing on Tuesday that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month. "Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort. We hope you will share our ambition to see it though."
